heading: Cold open
narration: The deep sea is not an empty black room with one anglerfish in it.

heading: Cold open
narration: It is open water, canyon walls, abyssal mud, seamounts, vents, whale falls, and trenches—each with a different community.

heading: Title card
narration: What creatures live in the deep sea?

heading: The right way to see it
narration: The answer changes with depth and terrain. Open midwater, continental slopes, abyssal plains, seamounts, vents, seeps, whale falls, and trenches support different communities.

heading: The right way to see it
narration: The rest of this video follows that question through the actual environmental constraints described by NOAA, MBARI, Smithsonian, and Woods Hole sources in the companion article.

heading: Producer POV
narration: Once I stopped building the list around thumbnail-friendly predators, the deep sea became much stranger: colonies, jellies, worms, microbes, scavengers, and animals that barely fit the categories we use on land.

heading: The deep sea is many habitats, not one empty place
narration: Open water below 200 meters covers an enormous volume, while the seafloor includes continental slopes, canyons, abyssal plains, seamounts and trenches.

args.caption: Open water below 200 metres covers an enormous volume

heading: The deep sea is many habitats, not one empty place
narration: Hydrothermal vents, cold seeps and whale falls create concentrated islands of food and chemical energy within the broader food-poor deep ocean.

heading: Twilight-zone animals
narration: Lanternfishes, bristlemouths, dragonfishes, squid, krill, siphonophores, jellies and zooplankton are common members of the mesopelagic community.

heading: Twilight-zone animals
narration: Many rise toward the surface at night and return to depth before daylight.

heading: Midnight and abyssal animals
narration: Anglerfishes, rattails, deep-sea squid, octopuses, sea cucumbers, amphipods, sponges, corals and gelatinous animals occupy the dark water column and seafloor.

args.title: THE DARK WATER COLUMN AND SEAFLOOR

heading: Midnight and abyssal animals
narration: Many depend on marine snow, scavenging, predation or chemosynthetic food webs.

heading: Hadal trench animals
narration: Trench communities include amphipods, sea cucumbers, worms, microbes and specialized snailfishes in the shallower portion of the hadal zone.

args.caption: Fish appear to have a physiological depth limit near 8,400 metres

heading: Hadal trench animals
narration: Fish appear to have a physiological depth limit near 8,400 meters, while invertebrates and microbes continue deeper.

heading: Common myths and questions
narration: A common question is: Do sharks live in the deep sea? Yes.

includes: Several shark species that use deep water
excludes: Present at the greatest trench depths

heading: Common myths and questions
narration: Several shark species use deep water, although sharks are not present at the greatest trench depths.

heading: Common myths and questions
narration: A common question is: Are there plants in the deep sea? Photosynthetic plants cannot grow where sunlight is absent. Deep ecosystems rely on food sinking from above or on chemosynthesis.

excludes: Photosynthetic plants, which cannot grow where sunlight is absent

heading: Common myths and questions
narration: A common question is: What is the most common deep-sea fish? Bristlemouths are often described as extraordinarily abundant and may be the most numerous vertebrates on Earth.

args.boundary: They may be the most numerous vertebrates on Earth

heading: Common myths and questions
narration: A common question is: How many deep-sea species are undiscovered? No reliable exact count exists. New species and previously unseen behaviors continue to be documented.

args.title: HOW MANY DEEP-SEA SPECIES ARE UNDISCOVERED?

heading: A tour organized by habitat, not celebrity
narration: Depth zones are useful labels, not sealed rooms. Animals migrate across boundaries.

heading: A tour organized by habitat, not celebrity
narration: Food falls through them. Currents transport particles and larvae. A whale carcass can connect surface productivity to the abyss.

heading: A tour organized by habitat, not celebrity
narration: Hydrothermal vents can support food webs based on chemical energy, while most of the deep ocean still depends ultimately on material produced above.

heading: A tour organized by habitat, not celebrity

heading: A tour organized by habitat, not celebrity
narration: This is why a single creature list always feels incomplete. The correct mental model is a network of habitats connected vertically and horizontally.

heading: A tour organized by habitat, not celebrity
narration: For retention, the episode should follow one unit of energy. Begin with surface production, let a particle sink, let a migrator carry carbon downward, let a predator take the migrator, let remains reach the bottom, and then show scavengers and microbes using what is left.

heading: The missing majority
narration: Any twenty-creature list will still leave out most of the deep ocean.

args.title: WHAT A TWENTY-CREATURE LIST LEAVES OUT

heading: The missing majority
narration: Microbes drive chemical transformations. Tiny crustaceans dominate many samples. Delicate gelatinous animals are underrepresented when nets destroy them.

heading: The missing majority
narration: Burrowing animals can remain invisible to cameras. Parasites and symbionts add relationships that a species list misses entirely.

args.title: WHAT A TWENTY-CREATURE LIST LEAVES OUT

heading: The missing majority
narration: The video should acknowledge that bias instead of using a handful of charismatic animals as the whole ecosystem.

heading: The missing majority
narration: One short sequence can compare methods: a net catches sturdy bodies, an ROV records behavior in a narrow lighted field, acoustics reveal movement at scale, and environmental DNA detects traces without showing the animal itself.

heading: The editorial rule for future additions
narration: A new creature enters this catalog only when it adds a habitat, ecological role, adaptation, or evidence method that the current set does not already explain.

heading: The editorial rule for future additions
narration: That rule prevents automation from producing twenty near-identical predator profiles. It also means microbes, scavengers, filter feeders, migrators, symbionts, and gelatinous animals must receive space beside the familiar thumbnail species.

narration: Use a map-like journey with a persistent depth and habitat label. Avoid rapid-fire stock montages that imply every animal shares the same water.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: No short episode can inventory the deep sea. Many species remain undescribed, and sampling is uneven across oceans and habitats.

heading: Closing
